**Mati Diop** (born 22 June 1982) is a French film director and actress. She won the [Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Prix_\(Cannes_Film_Festival\) "Grand Prix \(Cannes Film Festival\)") at the [2019 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Cannes_Film_Festival "2019 Cannes Film Festival") for her feature film debut, the supernatural romantic drama _[Atlantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantics "Atlantics")_ , and the [Golden Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Bear "Golden Bear") at the [2024 Berlin International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Berlin_International_Film_Festival "2024 Berlin International Film Festival") for her second feature film, the documentary _[Dahomey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey_\(film\) "Dahomey \(film\)")_. As an actress, she is known for the drama film _[35 Shots of Rum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/35_Shots_of_Rum "35 Shots of Rum")_ (2008).
## Early life
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mati_Diop&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]
Diop was born in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"). Her father, [Wasis Diop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasis_Diop "Wasis Diop"), is a black Senegalese musician, while her mother, Christine Brossard, is a white French art buyer and photographer. She is the niece of filmmaker [Djibril Diop Mambéty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djibril_Diop_Mamb%C3%A9ty "Djibril Diop Mambéty"). During her childhood, she often travelled back and forth between France and Senegal, developing a transnational identity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-1)
## Education
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mati_Diop&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]
Diop trained in the Advanced Degree Programme at Le Fresnoy National Studio of Contemporary Art in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-2) as well as at the [Palais de Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_de_Tokyo "Palais de Tokyo") in their experimental artist studio space Le Pavillon.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:0-3)
## Career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mati_Diop&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]
Diop was a fellow at the [Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radcliffe_Institute_for_Advanced_Study "Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study") from 2014 to 2015.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:0-3) Her work there focused on themes of exile, identity, memory, and loss, utilizing both fiction and documentary techniques.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-4) While a part of the institute's selective Film Study Center Fellowship Program, she wrote the script for her first feature film _Fire, Next Time._[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:0-3) She later changed the title of this film to what is now known as her directorial feature film debut, _[Atlantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantics "Atlantics")_ (2019).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:1-5)
In 2025, Mati Diop launched a U.S. university tour to present her documentary Dahomey, engaging in discussions on cultural restitution and decolonization. The tour included screenings and conversations at institutions such as Harvard University, Duke University, Columbia University, Pratt Institute, and Emory University.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-6)
### Directing
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mati_Diop&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Directing")]
Diop made her directorial debut in 2004 with her short film _Last Night_ (2004).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-7) Her short film _Atlantiques_ (2009) won the Rotterdam International Film Festival's Tiger Award for Short Film, and a Top Prize at Media City Film Festival[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-8) during her first North American appearance in 2009.
Her documentary short _Mille Soleils_[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-9) was released in 2013. The film focused on actor Magaye Niang, who was the star of Diop's uncle's seminal feature _[Touki Bouki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touki_Bouki "Touki Bouki")_ (1973) and explained how he had come to live as a farmer in the intervening years.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-10) The film played at the [2013 Toronto International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Toronto_International_Film_Festival "2013 Toronto International Film Festival") and was later also programmed at the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") in 2014.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:4-11)
In 2019, she became the first black female director to have her film premiere in competition at the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") when her feature debut _Atlantics_ was selected to compete for the [Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:1-5) She was one of only four women accepted into the festival in the given year.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:2-12) The film was a fictional adaptation of her documentary short _Atlantiques_ made in 2009 that followed two friends from Senegal as they made a life-threatening boat crossing to Europe.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:2-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-14) The film won the [Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Prix_\(Cannes_Film_Festival\) "Grand Prix \(Cannes Film Festival\)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-15) It was picked up by [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") shortly following Cannes' award announcements, however it is not a Netflix Original Film.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-16)
Diop directed a documentary, _[In My Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Tales "Women's Tales")_ , as part of Miu Miu's _[Women's Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Tales "Women's Tales")_ series, which blended audio recordings of her maternal grandmother, Maji, with footage Diop shot of herself in her Parisian apartment during the time she was quarantined during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic.
Diop's work has been featured at the [Venice Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Film_Festival "Venice Film Festival"), the [New York Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Film_Festival "New York Film Festival"), the [BFI London Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BFI_London_Film_Festival "BFI London Film Festival") in 2012, and the [Valdivia International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdivia_International_Film_Festival "Valdivia International Film Festival"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:0-3) as well as the [Museum of the Moving Image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_Moving_Image "Museum of the Moving Image") in 2013.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:4-11)
In 2024, she won the [Golden Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Bear "Golden Bear") at the Berlinale with the documentary, _[Dahomey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey_\(film\) "Dahomey \(film\)")_ , devoted to the question of the restitution by France of works of art stolen from Dahomey, present-day Benin.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-18)
### Acting
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mati_Diop&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Acting")]
Diop made her acting debut in [Claire Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claire_Denis "Claire Denis")' film _[35 Shots of Rum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/35_Shots_of_Rum "35 Shots of Rum")_ (2008), playing the lead role of a young woman in a close-knit relationship with her father, whom she has trouble leaving as she gets ready for marriage. She received a nomination for the [Lumière Award for Most Promising Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumi%C3%A8re_Award_for_Most_Promising_Actress "Lumière Award for Most Promising Actress") for her role in the film.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:4-11) In 2012, she appeared in the film _[Simon Killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Killer "Simon Killer")_ and was also credited with the story behind the script.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-19) Diop continues to act sporadically in films and television.
### Advertising
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mati_Diop&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Advertising")]
In 2026, Diop featured in an advertising campaign of [Phoebe Philo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoebe_Philo "Phoebe Philo")'s eponymous fashion brand.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-20)
## Artistry and themes
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mati_Diop&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Artistry and themes")]
In a 2025 interview with the _Financial Times,_ Diop discussed her cinematic approach, emphasizing the importance of centering African and diasporic narratives. She cited influences from American underground cinema, including filmmakers like Larry Clark and Harmony Korine, and highlighted her commitment to creating films that resonate deeply with African and Black audiences.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-21)
In their article on Diop's work up to _Atlantics_ (2019), Lindsay Turner states that Diop's work is often concerned with [trans-nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transnationalism "Transnationalism"), immigration, the female experience, and [post-colonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcolonialism "Postcolonialism")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-22) in relation with North Africa and Europe.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:7-23) In order to start work on _Atlantics_ , she began travelling to Senegal to reconnect with her African heritage. She says she found her voice in those journeys—and in her own French-Senegalese hyphenated identity.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-24) In an interview with _Metal Magazine_ , Diop explains that she tackles cinematics and poetic aspects of her film with different perspectives due to the contrasting "sensibilities" of French and African cultures.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-auto-25)
Diop uses aspects of magical realism in her films, examples including _Atlantics_ (2019), _Snow Cannon_ (2011), and _Big in Vietnam_ (2012).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-26) Diop can also be quoted talking about her storytelling processes, notably on how she uses sets and props to convey her plots as opposed to just characters and dialogue.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:7-23) During additional interviews, Diop has mentioned that she has done a majority of her own cinematography and is deeply interested in multiculturalism and multilingualism in film, as her films are often in two to three different languages.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-auto-25)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mati_Diop#cite_note-:7-23)
